items.title: The 107 vs 108 Scoring Bug in NIST 800-171 SPRS Calculators
items.summary: Most NIST SP 800-171 Rev. 2 controls are binary under DoD Assessment Methodology v1.2.1: you either show evidence and keep the points, or you subtract 5, 3, or 1 point from 110 (down to a floor of -203 across 313 total points). Only two controls allow partial credit, and they're the exact place online calculators get the math wrong: 3.5.3 (Multifactor authentication): 5-point control. If MFA is active for remote and privileged users, but not general local logins, DoD Methodology v1.2.1 deducts 3 points (so the control earns 2 of 5). 3.13.11 (FIPS-validated cryptography): 5-point control. If encryption is enabled without a FIPS 140-2/140-3 validated module, it also deducts 3 points (earning 2 of 5). When we first modeled those two controls in JSON, we accidentally stored partial.value = 3 (the deduction) in the points earned slot instead of 2. That meant a contractor with 109 controls fully met and only 3.5.3 partially implemented saw a score of 108 instead of 107. A reader flagged the mismatch, and cross-checking two independent primary sources confirmed the exact arithmetic: DoD Assessment Methodology v1.2.1 §5(a) & §5(e) specifies a 3-point deduction (110 - 3 = 107). 32 CFR 170.2

items.title: The security checklist I use on every Next.js app
items.summary: Residency Kondapur's platform stores tenants' names, phone numbers, rent bills and payment screenshots. That's the kind of data you can't treat as a side project. These are the protections I built into it, and now start every Next.js app with. Hash user passwords with bcrypt at cost 12. Never store them, never log them. Compare secrets in constant time. For the admin password I hash both the input and the stored value with SHA-256, then compare with crypto.timingSafeEqual. A plain === leaks timing information. One error message for every failure. "Authentication failed", never "wrong password" or "no such user". Don't tell an attacker which half they got right. Sign session tokens with HMAC-SHA256 so they can't be forged or edited. My format is a timestamp, some randomness, and a signature over both. Short lifetimes. Eight hours for admins, 24 for tenants. Cookies: httpOnly, SameSite=Strict, and Secure in production. JavaScript on the page can't read them, and other sites can't make the browser send them. Validate every body with Zod before it gets anywhere near the database. items.title: How to build a production-ready booking app in Next.js
items.summary: Building a booking app is harder than it looks. Beyond the basic calendar UI, you need to handle complex availability rules, timezone math, calendar integrations, payments, reminders, and a smooth admin experience. items.title: Demystifying Mongoose Connection Lifecycle & Auto-Reconnection in Node.js
items.summary: What Is the Mongoose Connection Lifecycle and Reconnection? The Mongoose connection lifecycle and reconnection refers to the sequence of stages a Node.js application moves through when establishing, maintaining, losing, and restoring its link to a MongoDB database. Mongoose is an Object Data Modeling (ODM) library, which is software that acts as an translator between Node.js code and a MongoDB database. Throughout this lifecycle, Mongoose continuously monitors the network channel and fires specific notification events whenever the state changes—such as when the database initially connects, experiences a unexpected disconnect, or successfully reconnects after a temporary outage. When a network blip occurs, Mongoose does not immediately crash your application. Instead, it enters a reconnection phase, automatically executing background retry attempts to re-establish communication without requiring an application restart. items.summary: My app had no users. My database was awake 720 hours that month. It was a staging environment for a multi-tenant commerce platform. No campaigns, no shoppers, no traffic. Neon's free tier gives you a monthly compute allowance, and serverless Postgres is supposed to auto-suspend after 5 minutes of inactivity. Two options hold up well: Fastify when you want raw throughput and JSON-schema validation built in. items.title: Stacking add-on licenses on one install
items.summary: A customer buys the base edition of your product. Six months later they buy an add-on pack that unlocks three more modules, and your fulfilment pipeline delivers it as a second signed key — not a reissue of the first. Now the installation holds two Keyright licenses at once. Next quarter an enterprise account stacks a site license with a per-seat top-up, and that is three. Your IsEnabled("analytics") was written against a single LicenseInfo. What does it even mean to ask whether a feature is enabled when the answer is spread across several independently-signed grants with different expiries — and one of them has just been revoked? The instinct is to pick one license as "primary" and treat the rest as patches. That instinct is wrong, and it gets worse every time you add a rule. The right model is algebraic: the effective license is a fold of every valid grant, under merge operators chosen so that the result cannot depend on the order the grants were processed in. items.title: Hunting Idunno.AntiCsrf (CVE-2026-131914) in Legacy ASP.NET Web Forms Apps
items.summary: Mandiant has warned that CVE-2026-131914, an insecure deserialization bug in Idunno.AntiCsrf 0.9.1.0 (a.k.a. 0.9.1 Beta), is being exploited in the wild. Reports put it at CVSS 9.3. The library's last official build is from December 2008 and it has no maintainer, so there is no patched version to upgrade to. If you look after old Web Forms apps, the job is to find it and remove it. The module's request handler deserializes the hidden _CSRFTOKEN form field before any authentication check. A POST with a CSRF cookie and a crafted payload in that field executes inside w3wp.exe. Because the module runs ahead of page code, any anonymous page (contact form, search, login) is a possible entry point. Pages configured to skip the CSRF check are reported as not exposed through this path. Grep each app's Web.config for AntiCsrfModule and Idunno.AntiCsrf. Check bin folders for the DLL, including staging copies and vendor-managed portals. Search by name rather than hash: recompiled copies bundled into other apps can have different hashes. items.title: How to Use SNS FIFO Topics for Ordered, Real‑Time Claude Code Suggestions, Explained Simply
items.summary: Claude just gave you a fresh piece of code—how do you get that suggestion to the right developers instantly without losing order? By publishing it to an SNS FIFO topic you can fan‑out reliably to Slack, a review Lambda, and a logging queue. This post shows you the exact steps, so you can trust the flow the first time. When an AI assistant like Claude spits out a series of suggestions, the order often carries meaning. The first suggestion might be a quick fix, the second a refactor, the third a performance tweak. If those messages arrive out of order, reviewers could waste time chasing a later suggestion that depends on an earlier one. FIFO stands for First‑In‑First‑Out. An SNS FIFO topic guarantees that subscribers receive messages in the exact sequence they were published, as long as they share the same MessageGroupId. Think of it like a line at a coffee shop: everyone gets their drink in the order they arrived, not in a random shuffle. In plain English: Using a FIFO topic makes sure “the code suggestion that came first is the one everyone sees first,” which is essential for deterministic CI pipelines. items.title: Decorators — Fastify with TypeScript (part 11/18)
items.summary: Decorators Eleventh chapter of the "Fastify with TypeScript" series. Decorators let you add your own properties and methods to the Fastify instance, the request, and the reply, in a fully type-safe way. We've been using one since chapter 4 without naming it: fastify.config. In this chapter we write another, to solve a problem the next chapter would otherwise run into. Our users live in an array declared inside the userRoutes plugin. That was the right place for it (chapter 5), but it means nothing outside that function can reach it. The next chapter adds an auth module with a login route, and login needs to look a user up by email. Two modules, one set of data: it has to live somewhere both can see. A global variable would do it, and we've already said why we don't want one. The Fastify answer is a decorator: attach the data to the instance, and every plugin that receives the instance can use it. items.summary: I wanted Claude and GitHub Copilot to answer questions from my own notes and documentation, without uploading anything. So I built docs-rag-mcp, an MCP server in C# that indexes a folder of documents and lets any MCP client search it. You point it at a folder of Markdown, text, HTML, Word or PDF files. It splits them into passages, embeds each passage, and stores everything in one SQLite file. When you ask your assistant a question, it calls search_docs and answers from the passages it gets back, with the file and section for each one. claude mcp add docs-rag -- dnx DocsRagMcp --yes With Ollama, nothing leaves your machine. It also works with OpenAI and Azure OpenAI embeddings. Getting a basic pipeline working is the easy part. Making the results good is harder, and that is what this post is about. items.title: Your Excel/VBA tool outgrew Excel: 6 signs to rebuild it as a desktop or web app (and what to keep)
items.summary: Your Excel macro runs the factory. Then the one person who understands it goes on holiday. Most small firms have a workbook like this. It started as a sheet to track orders, stock or shifts. Then it got macros, then forms, then a button that emails the weekly report. Now the business runs on it, and nobody wants to touch it. Excel is a good tool. Many workbooks should stay workbooks. But some reach a point where every week you keep them in Excel costs more than a rebuild. Here are six signs, and what to keep when you rebuild. "Can you close the file? I need to save." If people take turns, or keep their own copies and merge them on Friday, the workbook is acting as a database. It is not one. A shared app with a real database lets ten people work at once, and nobody overwrites anybody. The pricing logic, the discount rules, the way you plan production: they live in nested formulas and in VBA modules that one person wrote. If that person leaves, the rules leave too. An app does not fix this by itself. But a rebuild forces someone to write the rules down, and that alone lowers the risk. items.summary: Error handling Tenth chapter of the "Fastify with TypeScript" series. Good error handling is what separates a robust API from a fragile one. Our API currently produces errors in three different shapes, and one of them leaks information. Let's fix both by handling every error in one place. Fastify catches everything that is thrown in a hook or a handler and turns it into a response. To see what that response looks like, make a handler fail. In src/users/users.route.ts, add this as the second line of the GET / handler: throw new Error('connect ECONNREFUSED db-prod-01:5432 (user "admin")'); curl localhost:3000/api/v1/users # {"statusCode":500,"error":"Internal Server Error","message":"connect ECONNREFUSED db-prod-01:5432 (user \"admin\")"} The message of an internal error went straight to the client, host name and user included. Messages like this one are written for the developer who reads the log, and they routinely contain details an attacker would be glad to have. Leave the line where it is for a moment. setErrorHandler replaces the default behavior with a function of ours. items.summary: Hooks and the request lifecycle Ninth chapter of the "Fastify with TypeScript" series. Hooks are Fastify's equivalent of middleware, but with a well-defined execution order and much finer granularity. Rather than memorize that order from a diagram, we'll make the application print it. Every request goes through the same sequence of stages, and you can attach a function, a hook, to each of them: onRequest → preParsing → preValidation → preHandler → handler → preSerialization → onSend → onResponse Add this at the top of the userRoutes plugin in src/users/users.route.ts, just before the users array. items.summary: Plugins and encapsulation Eighth chapter of the "Fastify with TypeScript" series. The plugin system is arguably Fastify's most distinctive feature, and understanding encapsulation is essential to structuring any application well. We have been using a plugin since chapter 5 (userRoutes is one). In this chapter we write a second one, watch it fail in an instructive way, and fix it. A plugin is a function that receives a Fastify instance and adds things to it: routes, hooks, decorators, other plugins. You hand it to app.register(). The instance a plugin receives is not the root app. It is a child of it, and that is the whole point: what a plugin adds to its instance (hooks, decorators) exists inside that plugin and its own children, and nowhere else. This is encapsulation. Siblings don't see each other's hooks and decorators, and the parent doesn't see its children's. buildApp() in src/app.ts is getting crowded, and the OpenAPI setup from the previous chapter has nothing to do with the rest of it. items.summary: A motion alarm fires at 14:30:07 and the recorder starts writing at 14:30:07. items.title: I built an app that makes me solve a puzzle before opening social media
items.summary: I kept opening social media "for a second" — and losing 30 minutes. App blockers didn't work for me. One tap to dismiss, and they're off. The reflex was faster than my willpower. So I built Tokokage （やめトコカゲ in Japanese), a small iOS app that inserts one breath of friction: using a Shortcuts personal automation, when you try to open a social app, Tokokage launches first and asks you to clear a tiny puzzle — mini Sudoku, minesweeper, or a slide puzzle. Solve it and the social app opens. But most of the time, that pause is enough to make me think, "Did I actually want to open this?" — and put the phone down. It's deliberately not a hard block. No guilt trips, no locked phone. Just one puzzle between the reflex and the feed. Details: Free, with ads iOS 17 or later Setup: one Shortcuts personal automation per app you want to guard App Store: https://apps.apple.com/app/id6820095179 I originally built it for myself, but if your thumb also opens apps on its own, it might help you too. Feedback welcome — especially which puzzle type works best for you.

items.title: Azure DevOps Crash Course (Part 7): Docker, Azure Container Registry and Container Deployments
items.summary: The first time someone explained Docker to me, they said: "It is like shipping your laptop to production, but only the parts that matter." I laughed, but it stuck with me. Our Todo API currently runs on App Service with the .NET runtime that Azure provides. That works great. But sometimes you want full control over exactly what runs: the OS packages, the .NET version, everything. That is where containers come in. In Part 6 we sorted out configuration and secrets. Today we: Write a Dockerfile for the Todo API Build the image in Azure Pipelines Push it to Azure Container Registry (ACR) Run the container on App Service What you need to know before the code A Dockerfile is a recipe. Docker follows it and produces an image: your app plus everything it needs to run. A registry (we use Azure Container Registry) is a private storage place for images, like a private Docker Hub. App Service can pull an image from the registry and run it. Our pipeline just keeps the registry up to date. That is the whole idea. Everything below is just these three steps in practice. items.title: US Spy Agencies Suffer Breach of Some Unclassified Information
items.summary: An anonymous reader quotes a report from The New York Times: The Central Intelligence Agency and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence recently discovered a cybersecurity breach that exposed some of their unclassified information, according to U.S. officials and other people familiar with the matter. The intrusions affected an open-source intelligence analysis system, a computer network that looks for intelligence insights in public, unclassified material, the people familiar with the issues said. It was not clear specifically what information was compromised, but classified material was not jeopardized, the people said. Information at other government agencies was also believed to have been exposed in the breach, according to two of the people. Open-source intelligence can include vast troves of commercially available data sets, social media content, satellite imagery and other online material. Much of it is publicly available, but it can include information sold by data vendors that can be highly revealing, especially when combined with other tranches of data. Spy agencies can also use the data alongside other sources of intelligence to inform analytical judgments.

items.title: I Moved from Coding to Management. Then I Built a Teleprompter to Find My Next Line.
items.summary: I spent years writing code. Then I moved into management, and speaking in front of other people became a much bigger part of my job: team updates, work reports, sharing sessions. I knew the work. I could explain it in writing. But with everyone looking at me, I would get nervous, lose my train of thought, and suddenly forget what came next. That gap surprised me. Experience as a developer had not automatically prepared me to speak confidently about the work. So I approached one small part of the problem in a familiar way: I built a tool. It's called Oralo, a teleprompter that follows my voice. The goal was simple: when I lose my place, help me find the next line. Having a script gives me something to return to. But a teleprompter that scrolls at a fixed speed adds another thing to manage. I don't speak at a fixed speed. I slow down to explain a point. I pause. I add something that wasn't in the draft. When I come back, the text may already have moved on. Now I'm trying to do two things at once: talk to people and find my place on a moving page. items.title: I ported an Electron Starlink app to native Swift, then kept going
items.summary: I wanted my Starlink's latency and outages in the Mac menu bar, one glance away, without opening the phone app. The result is StarPulse, a free and open source (MIT) menu bar app written in Swift and SwiftUI. Repository and download: https://github.com/paulo-amaral/starlink-macos-menubar StarPulse started as a port of Dishylink by DaveyHert, an MIT-licensed Electron, React and TypeScript app for macOS, Windows and browsers. Dishylink worked out how to talk to the dish, which is the hard part. I wanted something that lived in the menu bar and felt like a Mac app, so I rebuilt it in Swift: Swift 6 and SwiftUI, macOS 14 or later, Apple silicon and Intel No third-party dependencies A 3.6 MB download 100 unit tests, runnable without any Starlink hardware Every Starlink dish answers a local API at 192.168.100.1:9201. It speaks gRPC-web over plain HTTP: a POST with a 5-byte frame header (one flag byte, four length bytes) followed by a protobuf message. The Starlink router answers the same protocol on port 9001 at your gateway. This post is about the things that went wrong and what I'd do differently. items.title: Endpoint Security on macOS without the entitlement: eslogger and Swift
items.summary: Endpoint Security is the macOS API that EDR products use to see every process launch, login and permission change. Using it directly requires an entitlement that Apple grants case by case. This post shows how MacSentry, my open-source Mac monitor, gets the same events through /usr/bin/eslogger instead, and what it took to make that fast and quiet: reading JSON Lines without parsing most of them, matching rules against the right program, and not alerting on itself. A native Endpoint Security client needs the com.apple.developer.endpoint-security.client entitlement, and Apple's documentation says plainly that you must request it. For a personal tool built from source, that is not realistic. macOS ships eslogger, a command-line Endpoint Security client that prints events as JSON Lines. MacSentry's helper, macsentry-es, is a root LaunchDaemon that starts eslogger with a list of event names and reads its standard output. The eslogger(1) man page sets the terms, and each one shaped the design: It must run as root, and the responsible process needs Full Disk Access. Because the helper launches eslogger as a child, macOS checks the helper's binary, so Full Disk Access goes to /usr/local/li

items.title: Using the language model built into iOS 26 for private, on-device chat
items.summary: Most AI chat apps send what you type to a server. On recent iPhones there is another option: Apple ships a language model inside iOS, and apps can use it without any network call. Secure AI is an iPhone and iPad app built on that. An iPhone or iPad with iOS 26 and Apple Intelligence. There is nothing to download besides the app, because the model is part of the OS. It is free to download, with in-app purchases. Older devices are not supported. Answers come from the model built into iOS, and a badge on each reply says it ran on device. There is no account to create. The app reads PDFs, scans and photos locally, including text inside pictures. Ask questions about a PDF and get answers that cite the passage they came from. Photograph a receipt and have the items read into a table, then split the bill. Use presets for different kinds of work. Chats are encrypted at rest by iOS. You can lock the app with Face ID, and export backups protected by a passphrase. The built-in model is smaller than the big cloud models, so expect weaker answers on hard reasoning or long, complex documents. The tradeoff is that your questions never leave the phone. More: https://secure.chinesepowered.com

items.summary: Hackers have compromised 24 Check Point Security management servers across 22 organizations in 17 countries in a suspected cyberespionage campaign, according to threat intelligence firm GreyNoise. BleepingComputer reports: The researchers track the activity as GT13 and confirmed it was ongoing between October 17 and November 2, when their visibility ended. However, given the threat actor's persistent access to Check Point devices, they believe the campaign remains active. GreyNoise says the 22 victim organizations are spread across 17 countries, and show no clear evidence of specific targeting. They include government entities, financial services providers, and companies in the energy, transportation, mining, and manufacturing sectors. The attacks were launched from 99 IP addresses that appear to come from compromised Check Point devices and ExpressVPN exit nodes. A Rejetto HTTP File Server, compromised by exploiting CVE-2026-61500, was used as an operational relay for managing intrusions and collecting stolen data from the compromised environments. While GreyNoise could not determine when or how the Check Point servers were breached, it observed the exploitation of CVE-2026-16232

items.summary: As I write this, my Mac has 7 dev servers listening on ports, two databases running, and a Next.js server on port 3000 holding 1.3 GB of memory. Everything it tracks adds up to 14.1 GB. I only know that because I built a menu bar app to tell me. It's open source, written in Swift, and it runs on macOS 13 or later. items.title: Porting a SwiftUI app to Rust and egui for Windows and Linux: what carried over and what didn't
items.summary: I wrote a Mac app in SwiftUI first. To bring it to Windows and Linux, I ported the UI to Rust with egui instead of reaching for a web view. The result is JoeBro Desktop (GPL-3.0, I made it), a single native binary. This is what carried over from SwiftUI, what had to be rebuilt by hand, and what I gave up. I wanted one small native program with no web runtime, the same on Windows and Linux (Wayland or X11), and a UI I could change quickly. egui is immediate mode: every frame you describe the UI with code and it draws it. There are no view objects to keep in sync with state, which suits an app where a lot of the screen is live data (agent sessions, streaming chat, approvals). The tradeoff is that egui draws everything itself. There are no native widgets, so the app won't pick up the system's look. For me that was a plus: I wanted the same design on both systems anyway, matching the Mac app. The Mac app has one file, JBDesign.swift, that holds every colour, radius, spacing step and font. I ported it nearly line for line into theme.rs. items.title: What I learned building Brimlight, a native macOS menu bar app with a 3D cat
items.summary: It launched on Product Hunt this week. Here's what building it taught me, from drawing behind menus to getting the first two sales. 1. The hardest feature is the one nobody notices: readable menus Painting something pretty behind the menu bar is easy. Keeping every menu title and status icon readable over 41 different animated themes, on any wallpaper, in Light and Dark mode, is not. What worked for me: Measure contrast where the text actually is. Not "is the theme dark on average", but "is it dark enough under this menu title right now". A bright pixel-art sunset can be fine on the left and unreadable under the clock. 2. No Screen Recording permission. Ever. The obvious way to "see" what's under the menu bar is to capture the screen. I made a rule on day one: Brimlight never asks for Screen Recording. Users get (rightly) nervous when a cosmetic app wants to see their screen. So the app reads what it legitimately can: the wallpaper image itself, the system appearance, and, only if the user turns it on, Accessibility data for the exact menu positions. items.title: Ladybird Web Browser/Engine Reaches Alpha
items.summary: The open-source Ladybird web browser has reached its alpha milestone after four years of development, offering an independent browser engine built from scratch rather than forked from Chromium, Firefox or another existing engine. Alpha builds are now available for macOS and Linux, including Flatpak packages and binaries for Ubuntu and Fedora. Phoronix reports: As for the expected alpha state: "Ladybird is a browser with a new engine. The engine is our own, built from the ground up, and not a fork. The browser around it is modest, but functional. This is an alpha, so some websites won't work, and it will crash sometimes. When that happens, tell us! You can report a broken site from inside the browser." Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: Recursive Self-Editing: LLMs Program Their Own Weight Edits for Self-Improvement (1 minute read)
items.summary: Today's language models improve themselves through data, training recipes, or scaffolds. Whenever their weights change, gradient descent writes the update, not the model. SELFWRITE lets the model write its own weights. Each generation, the current model studies its own reasoning on fresh training problems, inspects its own weights and activations in a persistent Python session, and writes a program that constructs a low-rank weight edit for itself from white-box primitives. It can raise gate accuracy and accuracy on a held-out test split that the loop never sees without a single gradient step.

items.title: Supercharging transformer residual connections (4 minute read)
items.summary: Google's DeepCrossAttention (DCA) enhances transformer residual connections by allowing each layer to dynamically select and route features from preceding layers, reducing information dilution and parameter count by 30-40%. Unlike traditional residual connections, DCA uses dynamic routing and depth-wise cross-attention mechanisms to achieve faster convergence and better quality with minimal parameter increase. Tested on large datasets like C4 and LM1B, DCA improves training efficiency and perplexity compared to standard models, proving a shift towards dynamic residual routing for scalable LLMs.

Scientists and doctors experimenting with gene editing use these natural self-editing and repair tools to insert, delete, or mutate genes to study and treat disease.

items.title: The Most Important Charts in AI are Wrong (35 minute read)
items.summary: AI capabilities are starting to become impressive. However, they are still dramatically inferior to what influential AI forecasts and benchmarks have predicted. These forecasts and benchmarks say that we are imminently close to reaching super-intelligence, but the gap between the real world and forecasts keeps growing larger. Now that real-world data exists, it's time to shift from being AI theorists to becoming AI empiricists.

items.title: AI x Bio is not _just_ a data problem (14 minute read)
items.summary: How far AI gets in biology will depend largely on how much data we have. It will also depend on what is measured and the quality of that data. An abundance of systematically incomplete measurements is unlikely to lead to a comprehensive understanding of many of the complex systems that occur in biology. AI will likely become a powerful tool that will contribute to the study of biology, but there is still no clear path to documenting a comprehensive account of how a whole cell or tissue works.

items.title: The most important number in AI (42 minute read)
items.summary: The Epoch Capabilities Index (ECI) is a measure of AI progress developed by Epoch AI, a nonprofit research organization. It provides a single number that summarizes how well AI models do on benchmarks. It is designed to be continuously updatable, and researchers can use it to look at trends going back years and forecast things for future models. This post covers how the ECI is constructed, the challenges of benchmark selection, whether it makes sense to talk about 'model IQ', whether static benchmarks stay relevant as models get better, and much more.

items.title: Unblockable communication with gravity (32 minute read)
items.summary: All modern wireless communication technologies are based on electromagnetism, which is readily susceptible to screening and blocking. Gravity is a viable platform for practically unblockable communication. This study proposes and implements a wireless communication protocol where a broadcaster encodes a binary message by moving a mass, and a receiver detects the resulting gravitational signal with an off-the-shelf, hand-held gravimeter.
